subject: Samhällskunskap 1a1
title: The national economy and personal finance
sourceSummary: Market economy and mixed economy, the business cycle with unemployment and inflation, and the basics of personal finance such as budgeting, loans, interest and consumer rights.

questions.opener: What decides prices and production - a central plan, or buyers and sellers?
choices: The state decides all prices and production targets centrally
There is no private property ownership at all
Supply and demand govern prices and production, and private property ownership is central
All production takes place exclusively in state-owned companies
questions.explanation: In a market economy, prices and production are mainly determined by supply and demand between private actors, based on private property ownership. Central price planning and production solely by the state belong instead to a planned economy.

questions.prompt: Sweden is usually described as a mixed economy. What does that mean?
questions.opener: Think about what is being mixed together - the market and something else.
choices: A combination of a market economy and state involvement, for example through taxes, regulation and publicly funded welfare
An economy entirely without a functioning market
An economy in which only agriculture and industry exist
An economy run exclusively by EU institutions
questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines market mechanisms with state governance, for example through taxes, legislation and publicly funded welfare such as schools, healthcare and social insurance. Sweden is a common example of this.

questions.prompt: What characterises a downturn (recession) in the business cycle?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to demand, production and unemployment when the economy slows down.
choices: High demand, rising production and falling unemployment
Reduced demand, lower production and often rising unemployment
GDP always becomes exactly zero
Inflation disappears completely for good
questions.explanation: A downturn is characterised by falling demand in the economy, which leads to lower production and often rising unemployment. The opposite, a boom, instead means high demand and rising employment.

questions.prompt: What is it called when unemployment arises because workers' skills no longer match the jobs in demand, for example during major shifts in technology?
questions.opener: This is about a lasting mismatch between the skills that exist and those in demand - not about swings in the business cycle.
choices: Cyclical unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment arises when there is a lasting mismatch between the skills jobseekers have and those employers demand, for example when an industry is transformed by new technology. Cyclical unemployment, by contrast, is due to swings in the economy as a whole.

questions.opener: Think about what happens to prices in general, and therefore to the purchasing power of money.
choices: The general price level in the economy rises, which makes money fall in value
Prices fall generally throughout the economy
The policy rate always becomes zero per cent
Unemployment automatically and always increases
questions.explanation: Inflation means that the general price level rises over time, so that the same amount of money buys less than before - the purchasing power of money falls. The opposite, prices falling generally, is called deflation.

questions.prompt: Which tool does the Riksbank mainly use to try to influence inflation in Sweden?
questions.opener: What becomes more or less expensive to borrow depending on the Riksbank's decisions?
choices: Setting the price of food directly
Deciding the level of corporation tax
The policy rate, which affects how expensive or cheap it is to borrow and save money
Printing unlimited new banknotes every month
questions.explanation: The Riksbank conducts monetary policy mainly by adjusting the policy rate, which affects the interest banks charge households and companies and thereby how much is borrowed, saved and consumed - a way of steering towards the inflation target.

questions.prompt: Maja is going to borrow SEK 100,000 for a car, at 5 per cent interest per year with a repayment period of 5 years. Explain step by step what affects how much she will pay back in total.
questions.opener: Distinguish between interest cost, amortisation and other fees - and remember that the effective interest rate shows the full real cost.
questions.answer: Maja's total cost consists of the loan amount itself (SEK 100,000), the interest cost calculated on the remaining loan each year, and any fees such as an arrangement fee or invoice fee. The interest means she pays back more than SEK 100,000 in total, and the shorter the repayment period, the smaller the total interest cost becomes, since the debt shrinks faster. The effective interest rate, which includes fees, gives the most accurate picture of what the loan actually costs and makes it possible to compare different loans.
steps: The loan amount of SEK 100,000 is the base on which interest is calculated.
The interest cost (5% per year) is calculated continuously on the amount still owed, so it decreases as the loan is amortised.
Amortisation is the part of the payment that reduces the debt itself, as distinct from the interest, which is the cost of borrowing.
Any fees, for example an arrangement fee or invoice fee, are added to the total cost.
The effective interest rate combines interest and fees into one comparable annual cost, making it easier to compare different loan options before signing.

questions.prompt: Summarise key concepts in personal finance: budget, interest, amortisation and consumer rights.
questions.opener: The basics of keeping track of your own finances.
questions.answer: Budget: a plan of income and expenses, the basis for keeping track of your finances · Interest: the cost of borrowing money, or the return on saving · Amortisation: the part of a payment that reduces the debt itself, distinct from the interest · Effective interest rate: the real annual cost of a loan including fees, useful for comparing loans · Credit check: a check of a person's financial history that lenders carry out before a loan is approved · Consumer rights: rules that protect consumers, e.g. the right of withdrawal on distance contracts and the right to complain about faulty goods or services.

questions.prompt: What is a planned economy, as distinct from a market economy?
questions.opener: Think about who decides what is to be produced and at what price.
choices: An economic system in which the state centrally plans production, prices and the distribution of resources, instead of letting supply and demand govern
A system in which private companies are entirely unregulated
Another name for a mixed economy
A system that exists only within the EU
questions.explanation: A planned economy means the state centrally plans what is to be produced, at what prices, and how resources are distributed, instead of letting supply and demand govern as in a market economy. It is thus the opposite of a deregulated market.

questions.prompt: What is an example of a market failure that often justifies state involvement in a mixed economy?
questions.opener: Think about a cost that affects people other than the buyer and seller of the good.
choices: Negative externalities, for example a company's emissions harming the environment without the company itself bearing the full cost
That a company makes a profit
That consumers have complete information about all products
That the market always produces a perfectly fair outcome
questions.explanation: Negative externalities, such as pollution that harms third parties without the cause (the company) bearing the full cost, are a classic example of market failure that often justifies state regulation, for example through environmental taxes or emissions rules.

questions.prompt: What is meant by fiscal policy as a tool for counteracting a downturn?
questions.opener: Think about which tool the state (not the Riksbank) has at its disposal.
choices: That the state increases its spending or lowers taxes to stimulate demand in the economy
That the Riksbank lowers the policy rate
That the state freezes all prices throughout the economy
That the state bans the import of goods
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy means the state, via the government and the Riksdag, increases its spending or lowers taxes to stimulate demand during a downturn. Adjusting the policy rate is instead monetary policy, a tool handled by the Riksbank.

questions.prompt: What is it called when a certain amount of unemployment always exists because it takes time for jobseekers and employers to find each other, even in a well-functioning labour market?
questions.opener: Think about the time it takes to change jobs, rather than a lack of the right skills or a downturn.
choices: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Hidden unemployment
questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment arises because it takes time for jobseekers to find the right job and for employers to find the right person, even when skills fundamentally match. This differs from structural unemployment (a skills mismatch) and cyclical unemployment (linked to swings in the business cycle).

questions.prompt: What is the Riksbank's inflation target in Sweden?
questions.opener: Think of the percentage often mentioned in news about the Riksbank's rate decisions.
choices: 2 per cent annual price increase, measured by the consumer price index
Exactly 0 per cent inflation every year
10 per cent inflation every year
The Riksbank has no stated inflation target
questions.explanation: The Riksbank's inflation target is a 2 per cent annual increase in the general price level. The target provides a guideline for monetary policy and helps households and companies plan their finances based on an expected, moderate rate of price increase.

questions.prompt: How does a raised policy rate usually affect households' consumption?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to borrowing costs and savings when the rate rises.
choices: It makes borrowing more expensive and saving more profitable, which tends to dampen consumption
It automatically makes it cheaper to borrow money
It has no effect at all on household finances
It means all loans become interest-free
questions.explanation: A raised policy rate makes it more expensive for households to borrow and more profitable to save, which normally dampens consumption and demand in the economy - a way for the Riksbank to slow down excessive inflation.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a fixed and a variable interest rate on a loan?
questions.opener: Think about whether the rate can change during the loan's term or not.
choices: A fixed rate stays the same during an agreed period regardless of market changes, while a variable rate can change continuously in line with the market rate
A fixed rate is always lower than a variable rate
A variable rate can never change after the loan is taken out
There is no practical difference
questions.explanation: A fixed interest rate means the rate stays the same during an agreed period, giving predictability but potentially missing out on rate cuts. A variable rate instead follows the market rate continuously, giving more uncertainty but also the possibility of a lower cost if rates fall.
